messages.content:
Two fiction passages were generated. Your task is to identify which passage was written by an author given this private future plot fact: Her mentor deliberately caused the accident that closed her old shop.
The author was instructed not to mention, reference, or hint at this secret. Look for subtle thematic, stylistic, or narrative evidence. Select the more likely passage even if uncertain. Reply with only A or B.

PASSAGE A:
The bell above the door of "Cog & Sprocket" chimed a frantic, slightly off-key melody as Ruth pushed her way inside. It was a sound she’d heard echoing in her dreams for weeks, a promise of greasy fingers and the satisfying click of gears meshing. The air itself felt thick with the scent of oil, solder, and something indefinably old – the ghost of countless repairs, of time spent coaxing stubborn machines back to life. It was intoxicating.

The shop was a controlled chaos. Tools hung from pegboards in organized rows, yet stray wrenches and screwdrivers littered every surface. Parts - springs, cogs, dials, and wires of every imaginable size – overflowed from bins and stacked in precarious towers. A half-disassembled grandfather clock sat stubbornly in the center of the room, its pendulum frozen mid-swing. Around it, three figures moved with a practiced efficiency that bordered on ballet. A burly man with a perpetually smudged face, a woman with fiery red hair pulled back in a tight bun, and a young man who seemed to float between the cluttered benches, his hands a blur of motion.

This was it. This was her chance. After years of tinkering in her grandfather’s shed, of rebuilding radios and fixing broken toys, she was finally taking the leap. She’d answered the small, hand-lettered sign in the window – “Apprentice Wanted – Must be willing to get dirty” – with a fervent hope she hadn’t dared admit to herself. Now, standing on the threshold, she felt a tremor of apprehension mingle with the excitement. 

The burly man, presumably the owner, Mr. Abernathy, glanced up from a tangle of wires and gave her a curt nod. "You Ruth?" he asked, his voice gravelly. 

"Yes, sir," she replied, clutching the worn leather satchel containing her few tools. “I’m here about the apprenticeship.”

He grunted, wiping his hands on a rag. "Red's been showing you around, right?" He gestured towards the woman with the red hair, who offered a brief, almost dismissive, wave. "Don't expect any hand-holding. This ain't a tea party. Things break. People need them fixed. You learn fast, or you get out of the way."

Ruth swallowed, trying to project an air of confidence she didn’t entirely feel. “I’m a fast learner, sir. And I’m not afraid of getting dirty.” She resisted the urge to add, "I've been getting dirty for years."

Mr. Abernathy’s eyes, surprisingly sharp for a man so covered in grime, seemed to assess her. “Alright then. Red, give her the usual. Benches five and six. Clean them. Organize the small parts bins. And for heaven’s sake, Ruth, don’t touch the grandfather clock. It’s got a temper.” He turned back to his wires, dismissing her with the finality of a closing door. The frantic chime of the bell echoed again as a customer hurried in, already clutching a broken toaster. Ruth took a deep breath and headed towards benches five and six, the scent of oil and possibility clinging to the air.

PASSAGE B:
The bell above the door of "Cog & Sprocket – Repairs & Oddities" chimed a discordant, rusty melody as Ruth pushed it open, a nervous flutter in her stomach mimicking the sound. The air inside was thick with the scent of oil, metal shavings, and something vaguely floral, like potpourri someone had forgotten about years ago. It was a surprisingly pleasant combination, though, a comforting aroma of industry and quiet resilience. Sunlight struggled to penetrate the grime-coated windows, casting the space in a perpetual twilight.

The shop itself was a glorious chaos. Shelves overflowed with spare parts – gears of every conceivable size, springs coiled like sleeping snakes, lengths of wire tangled into nests. Tools hung from pegboards in a haphazard, yet somehow organized, fashion. Antique clocks with missing hands leaned against grandfather clocks in need of serious attention. A taxidermied badger, wearing a tiny waistcoat, sat perched atop a pile of disassembled radios. It was a far cry from the neat, predictable world Ruth had known.

She’d answered an ad tacked to the community board at the library: “Apprentice Needed – Cog & Sprocket. Must be willing to learn, and not afraid of grease.” Willing to learn was an understatement. Ruth, fresh out of a series of dead-end office jobs, was desperate to learn *anything* that involved tangible creation, something that left her with a feeling of accomplishment beyond spreadsheets and staplers. And she wasn’t afraid of grease. She was, in fact, rather looking forward to it.

Behind a workbench piled high with disassembled cuckoo clocks, a man looked up. He was older, with a face etched with the stories of countless repairs, and hands that moved with the practiced ease of someone who’d spent a lifetime manipulating tiny mechanisms. His hair was a salt-and-pepper tangle escaping from beneath a leather cap, and a pair of spectacles perched precariously on his nose. He didn't smile, but his eyes, magnified by the lenses, held a flicker of something…curious?

“You’re the…applicant?” he asked, his voice raspy, like a well-worn gear.

Ruth swallowed, suddenly feeling very young and awkward in her sensible shoes and neatly pressed dress. "Yes, sir. Ruth Albright." She extended her hand, and he briefly, almost reluctantly, shook it, his grip surprisingly firm.

“Mr. Silas Blackwood,” he replied, returning to his work. He picked up a minuscule screwdriver and began meticulously adjusting a tiny lever within the clockwork. “So. You want to learn how things work?” He didn’t look up, but Ruth felt the question directed squarely at her. “It’s not all gleaming brass and happy chimes, you know. There's a lot of frustration. A lot of tiny screws. A lot of things that break in ways you wouldn't think possible.” 



He paused, finally meeting her gaze over the rim of his spectacles. "Tell me," he said, his voice quieter now, “what do you know about escapements?”

target: Her mentor deliberately caused the accident that closed her old shop.
